role: biologist, Joseph LeConte Chapter, Sierra Club
stance_basis: closes letter with 'emphatic opposition to the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project'
summary: John J. Hagins, a biologist and member of the LeConte Chapter of the Sierra Club, submitted detailed written comments opposing the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project on behalf of the Chapter, raising concerns about the saddle dike fuse design, wildlife and fishery impacts, energy waste, conservation alternatives, piecemeal environmental assessment, and the project's overall economic and environmental detriments. He followed up with a second letter enclosing a memo to Duke Power's Dr. L.L. Olmsted that elaborated on energy efficiency calculations and argued that peak demand elimination through rate restructuring was a superior alternative. He concluded with emphatic personal opposition, stating the project would be detrimental to the land, people, economy, and Duke Power itself.
complaint_summary: In a memo/letter to Duke Power's Warren H. Oven (Dr. L.L. Olmsted), Hagins argues that the project wastes 1.3 million MMH of electricity annually (equivalent to the total annual consumption of over 121,000 homes), that conservation and peak-demand elimination through rate restructuring are superior alternatives, that the environmental degradation of a unique natural area and fishery cannot be justified by mere convenience, and that he stands in emphatic opposition to the project.

statement.text:
January 28, 1976
Length to D. LL. Dlom, ted
Meno to: Herren-H. Oven-
Subject: Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project
GS-110.10
For the past three years I have been sware of the Company's plans for pumped storage development in the valleys of the Blue Ridge escarpment in the vicinity of Lake Jocassee. In as much as possible, I have tried to follow arguments both pro and con concerning this particular development. As the issue has been represented, the reason for this development is to provide storage capacity for a subsequent peak demand. The energy for such storage would be drawn from existing baseline generation facilities during off peak periods. This peaking power capability is the preponderance of the benefit in any cost/benefit analysis. In general, according to the application for license, this facility will operate approximately 7000 hours annually. Approximately 2500 hours of generation will be expected annually. Of course most of this peaking power will be generated during periods in which the weather is at annual temperature extremes; this also being discussed in the application for license. I feel that the causative agents for peak demands are familiar enough not to warrant discussion. If one assumes that this and existing facilities are adequate to meet demand - then the benefit is clear.
Being familiar with the area of this development, I can appreciate the environmental impacts discussed both in the license and in the Draft Environmental Impact Statement. Briefly, a portion of essentially unused, unoccupied land in nearly its natural state will be used and inundated by the reservoir, generation facilities and rights of way. This will be constructed through and into an area of such size and beauty that may render it unique in lands other than parks or National Forests. Wildlife, both flora and fauna, will be displaced or destroyed. Habitat for unique forms will be lost. That same habitat could also support other species that are being restored after depletion due to past impacts by man. An integral part of the fishery of Lake Jocassee will be impacted by the construction of this development.
The justification of such a trade-off is the focus of this letter. The Company has made its predictions of future peak demands. However, as I write this letter it will have been approximately two years since the submission of those predictions. In view of recent changes of factors affecting such a prediction, are these still accurate?

Warren H. Oven
Alternatives to this development have been considered in the Draft Environmental Impact Statement. Host of those alternatives involve some type of additional power generation which for economic and, at times, environmental reasons are undesirable. The only nongeneration alternative considered was that of conservation and rate revision. Duke Power had no consideration of conservation and rate revision as an alternative in Section 8.2 of its application for license before the FPC. The FPC could not determine quantitatively the effects of such measures and/or the price elasticity of demand. Therefore, the FPC dismissed conservation and rate revision as a reasonable alternative while urging the vigorous pursuit of such measures. I submit that if this development were built and such measures were successful, the land would still have the impact and the Company would have an unnecessary investment.
From Exhibit 1 in the application for license, data is given that supports the following conclusions. This facility is capable of continuous full load operation for 32 hours. The continuous pumpback to full pond will require 45 hours. Therefore, each 32,000 MMH of electricity generated will require 45,000 MMH of pumpback energy with a resulting efficiency of 71.1%. Annual total operating time will be 7000 hours. Approximately 2500 hours of that time will represent peneration on demand at the full rated capacity. The plant will therefore be in some phase of full capacity operation for approximately 80% of the year. The annual pumpback time will be equivalent to 4500 hours or approximately 100 complete pumpback cycles. With 13,000 MMH wasted on each pumpback, the result will be an annual waste of 1,300,000 MMH of electricity.
On the basis of the average consumption per household listed for Duke Pover's customers through October 31, 1974, the annual waste at Bad Creek would provide one month's electrical energy for 1,454,545.4 homes. On the same basis the annual waste at Bad Creek would provide for the total annual consumption for 121,212.1 homes. There were 951,459 residential customers on January 1, 1975.
To put this in mother perspective, the annual waste at Bad Creek represents 84.3% of the total annual generation of Duke Power conventional hydro units at median streamflow conditions. In other words, neglecting the lands inundated by smaller impoundments and based on the total surface acreages for impoundments on the Catawba River and Lake Keowee, the waste at Bad Creek will negate the hydroelectrical benefit for which 83,174 acres of land were flooded.
The conflict is obvious. The more Bad Creek operates the more energy is vasted. The less it operates the more difficult to justify economically.

3
The best alternatives are to find other energy efficient nonpolluting sources or to eliminate the peaks. In view of the alternatives listed in the application for license, the elimination of peak demand is the better alternative.
I understand that study of peak pricing is currently underway in the Duke Power system. The price elasticity of demand will be the determining factor of the study's success. It is possible that revision of the basic rate structure to the point that increased usage increases unit price will enhance the concept of peak pricing.
It should be possible to raise demand during off peak periods in order to "even out" the demand curve by offering power to some large users on an agreed interruptable basis in return for a lower price. The price would be lowered by an amount corresponding to the extra cost of producing power for the peaks. Not all customers could accept an interruptable source, but the amount of power available for production would be increased, in essence, by the amount that would have been wasted by Bad Creek and other pumped storage facilities. This would increase productivity, employment, efficiency of the economy, and Duke Power would not have invested in an energy wasting device. It is within the purposes for which the corporation is organized as set forth in the Articles of Incorporation of Duke Power Company to, if necessary, build and operate such facilities themselves. Of course this would mean an investment, but environmental impact would be minimized, the economy would gain, and energy derived from environmentally degrading sources would be put to use, not to waste.
As a biologist it is enough that Bed Creek threatens a natural area, the environmental integrity of a larger area, a fishery, and the existence of several unique forms. I could oppose most developments on those grounds alone. Peak demand is one thing, need for energy another. The resolution of the two concepts is a moral issue that has yet to be decided. But to allow that environmental degradation and the energy waste inherent in its design for the sake of convenience is intolerable.
I hereby stand with emphatic opposition to the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project as in the long run it will be detrimental to the best interests of the land, the people, the economy, and therefore, Duke Power Company.
John J. Hagins
(Biologist/ Environmental Laboratories
